Omar Bradley spent World War One guarding copper mines in Montana while his classmates went to France. Twenty-eight years later he commanded four American armies, and history gave the credit to louder men.

He was the farm boy from Missouri who worked as a railroad boilermaker for seventeen cents an hour, graduated in the middle of West Point's "class the stars fell on," and did not see combat until he was fifty. videos.title: Zhukov’s Top 3 Legendary Tactical Moves | Why Stalin Exiled His Best General
videos.desc:
#Zhukov #MilitaryHistory #EasternFront

Georgy Zhukov stopped Hitler at the gates of Moscow, broke Army Group Center, and took Berlin. A year after he reviewed the Victory Parade, Stalin sent him into exile.

In June 1946, Stalin had charges read against him before the Main Military Council: arrogance, disloyalty, claiming too much credit for the victory. The most famous soldier in the Soviet Union was stripped of command and sent to Odessa, then to the Urals. Investigators counted his war trophies down to the furs, a strange detail for a man who began life as a furrier's apprentice.

videos.title: Manstein's Top 3 Genius Moves | The Plan They Tried to Bury
videos.desc:
#Manstein #MilitaryHistory #WW2
In the winter of 1939, one staff officer wrote the plan that would defeat France in six weeks. His own superiors blocked it, then sent him away to command an infantry corps on the Baltic.

Erich von Manstein sent at least six memoranda up the chain at Army Group A. None reached Hitler. It took a crashed courier plane, two loyal former staff officers and a lunch at the Reich Chancellery before his idea became the German plan for 1940. He spent the decisive days of that campaign far from the front, watching his plan unfold from a distance.

videos.title: Montgomery’s Top 3 Genius Moves | The General Who Ended Germany’s Winning Streak
videos.desc:
#Montgomery #WW2 #MilitaryHistory

Bernard Montgomery beat Rommel in the desert and commanded every Allied soldier on the ground in Normandy. By January 1945, America's leading field general was telling Eisenhower he could not serve under him.

He was vain, tactless, and maddeningly slow, and the Americans who fought beside him never forgave his habit of taking the credit. But the record tells a story his critics rarely finished. videos.desc:
Erwin Rommel was the general his enemies admired most. In October 1944, the regime he served handed him a capsule of poison, then gave him a state funeral and blamed his wounds.

The British spent two years saying his name with something close to awe. Their commander in the Middle East ordered his officers to stop calling him a magician. Their Prime Minister called him "a great general" in the House of Commons while the war was still undecided. videos.title: Eisenhower's Top 3 Genius Moves | The General Who Never Saw Combat
videos.desc:
#MilitaryHistory #DDay #Eisenhower

Dwight D. Eisenhower never led troops in combat, and Britain's top soldier wrote that he was hopeless as a general. He went on to command the largest invasion in history and the armies that broke Hitler in the West.

His orders to sail for France came through in October 1918. The war ended seven days before he was due to leave. He then spent sixteen years as a major, wrote speeches for Douglas MacArthur, and opened his own war with the American defeat at Kasserine Pass.

videos.desc:

videos.title: Heinz Guderian's Top 3 Legendary Tactical Moves | Fired for Being Right
videos.desc:
Heinz Guderian broke the French Army in 1940 and helped trap an entire Soviet army group in 1941. On Christmas 1941, he was sent home in disgrace for pulling his freezing soldiers back from ground they could not hold.

He was a signals officer who did not sit inside a tank until 1929. By 1937 he had written the book on armoured warfare. In May 1940 his panzers crossed the Ardennes, a forest the French high command called impenetrable, and forced the Meuse at Sedan in 57 hours. Six days later they were standing on the English Channel.

Washington's army was outflanked at the Jamaica Pass, pinned against the East River at Brooklyn Heights, and chased the length of New Jersey.
